content.text:
**One press a Round.** [PR #268](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/268), auto-merge armed.

You were right that the first click did nothing. It was a button labelled with the table's own title (`Club Standard`), which is why it read like a mode switch — `rollTable` steps fall back to the table title when they have no label, and with Auto-roll on the press meant "go" and nothing else.

## `unit.handsFree`

```yaml
capabilities: [handsFree]
unit:
  handsFree: true
```

A step that asks you nothing before it runs starts itself when the Round opens, so the call is just there. Reading it closes the Round and opens the next. Declared on the pack, overridable per mode, with a capability entry so an older build refuses the pack rather than playing it at three times the presses.

## What I checked in the app, not in my head

I played to Round 20. Ten consecutive `Carry on` presses gave ten Rounds, no drift.

The interesting one was **Round 12**, where Soundclash's own counter threshold fires. The run stopped dead for it: the receipt's onward doors withdrew and `The game has your number — Twelve in` was the only thing to press. That's the guard doing its job — a threshold, an owed obligation, a confirm point, a declaration each hold the Round. Applying it put the loop straight back to one press.

Two others:

- **Auto-roll off isn't a special case.** The step still starts itself and you land on the dice tray, so physical-dice players save the same press. Cancelling drops back to the ordinary step card and doesn't spin — a step auto-starts once per unit and is remembered.
- **"Carry on by itself" is suppressed** when the press would close the unit. That 1.8s timer plus this would have played your whole set with nobody in the room. Worth knowing that's why: it's also what flattered my count last time and made me report two presses when you were seeing three.

Since the receipt is now the whole Round, it carries the fork the closing step used to: `Carry on` and `Finish the set`.

## Two things I fixed along the way

`0 tracks made so far` on the between-units card, on a pack that makes no tracks. It counts units there now — "19 rounds so far". Same family as the board panel from #267.

And I re-ran **Forfeits** in the browser to be sure nothing leaked: roll step still waits for its button, board panel still there, three phases in the rail. Unchanged.

Soundclash itself is now a single `Mix it` step holding the four style rolls, each skipped outside its own mode — the rail shows one step because there is one.

# First of the checks, because it is the cheapest and it fails for
      # a reason none of the others can catch: a pack edited in place at
      # the version it already had reaches a library by id and version,
      # so nobody holding the old one is ever offered it. It used to run
      # after the suite, which meant waiting a minute and a half to be
      # told to change one line.
      #
      # Asked of the pull request, where there is a before to compare
      # against; the merge queue has already asked it of each one.
      - name: A changed pack says so in its version
        if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
        env:
          BASE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        run: |
          git fetch --no-tags --depth=1 origin "$BASE"
          npm run check:pack-versions -- "$BASE"

      - run: npm run typecheck

| Rocket League: Showdown | Implicitly — "One person moderates…" |
| Practice Room, Ladder Work, Run of Show, Twenty-five, TarnishedTool | No — activity only |

(`ladder-work` looked broken in my first pass; that was my extraction script running past a blank line. The file is fine.)

## Hooks: yes, but not as a pre-commit, and lint-staged has nothing to do here

**There is no formatter or linter in this repo.** devDeps are `@types/node, ajv, ajv-formats, esbuild, fake-indexeddb, jsdom, markdownlint-cli2, typescript, vitest`. No prettier, no eslint. No `.husky`, no installed hooks, `core.hooksPath` unset.

That matters, because **lint-staged's whole job is running a rewriting tool over just the staged files** — `prettier --write`, `eslint --fix`. With no such tool, it has nothing to call. Adding one is a much bigger decision than this: prettier would rewrite every file in the repo once, and this codebase has a deliberate hand-written style (the doc comments especially) that I wouldn't put through a formatter without you asking for it.

**markdownlint doesn't need lint-staged either.** `lint:docs` already globs the repo and finishes in about a second across 18 files. Restricting it to staged files saves nothing and adds partial-stage edge cases. Just run the whole thing.

**The version check should be `pre-push`, not `pre-commit.`** Its question is "does this branch say something different from its base" — a branch-level question, not a per-commit one. As a pre-commit it would fail on *every* commit from the first edit until you bumped, which trains you to `--no-verify`. At pre-push it runs once, at the moment the answer stops being hypothetical. It also wants the real merge-base rather than assuming `origin/main` is current, so the hook should `git fetch` first — otherwise it compares against a stale ref and passes when CI won't.

**`simple-git-hooks` over husky** for this: one small dependency, config in `package.json`, no `.husky/` directory of shell scripts. Husky's advantages are for many hooks and many contributors; you have two hooks and one contributor.

Worth saying plainly: hooks only exist after `npm install` runs, and `--no-verify` skips them. CI stays the authority — this is a faster feedback loop, not a gate.

asked for, so the setup screen carried two checkboxes for one piece of
equipment.

So `decks` says what it always meant, and `vinyl` is gone. The needle
drop was the only result leaning on it; it now says what to do rather
than what to do it on.

| `tt-08` | Needle drop. Find the spot by eye, no cue point. | Drop in by eye. Find the spot on the platter yourself, no cue point. |

Also strips trailing whitespace from the description, which came from an
editor rather than a decision.

0.3.0: one fewer thing asked at setup, and a result that no longer draws
again for anybody.

1160 tests, 4 fixtures play, pack validates strict.

content.text:
Answering your three, because the third one changes my recommendation.

**1. Yes, lint-staged needs a config** — I hadn't written it yet, I was still measuring.

**2. `simple-git-hooks` generates `.git/hooks/pre-commit` directly** when you run it, rather than using a `.husky/` directory. That's why you don't see one.

**3. And that's exactly its weakness.** Hooks it writes are untracked files in `.git/`, invisible in the repo, propagated only by a `postinstall` that `npm ci --ignore-scripts` skips silently. Husky's whole design is the opposite: hooks are **tracked files in `.husky/`**, `core.hooksPath` points at them, and npm's `prepare` lifecycle activates them on install. For a public repo with contributors that's the better trade, and my earlier recommendation weighted "lightweight" over "propagates", which was the wrong way round. Switching to husky.

Two measurements worth having first:

content.text: Now the hooks and configs.

input.command:
cat > .husky/pre-commit <<'SH'
# Format what is being committed, and nothing else.
#
# lint-staged runs the formatter over the staged files only and restages
# what it changed, so a commit is formatted without touching work still
# in the working tree.
npx lint-staged
SH
cat > .husky/pre-push <<'SH'
# A pack that changed says so in its version.
#
# CI asks this of a pull request, where there is a base to compare
# against. That is the right place for the gate and the wrong place to
# find out: the answer is a one-line edit, and hearing it two minutes
# into a workflow run is how it gets missed. So it is asked here too,
# at the last moment it is still cheap to fix.
#
# Pushing is also the first moment the question is answerable. A branch
# is many commits, and asking it of each one fails on every commit
# between the first edit and the bump, which teaches you --no-verify.
remote_main="$(git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/remotes/origin/main || true)"
if [ -z "$remote_main" ]; then
  echo "pre-push: no origin/main to compare against; skipping the pack version check."
  exit 0
fi

# Against the merge base rather than the tip, so a main that has moved on
# is not mistaken for this branch having changed something.
git fetch --no-tags --quiet origin main || echo "pre-push: could not reach origin; comparing against the origin/main already here."
base="$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)"
npm run --silent check:pack-versions -- "$base"
SH
node -e "
const fs=require('fs'); const p=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('package.json','utf8'));
p.scripts.format = 'prettier --write .';
p.scripts['format:check'] = 'prettier --check .';
const {prepare, ...rest} = p.scripts;
p.scripts = { prepare, ...rest };
p['lint-staged'] = {
  '*.{ts,tsx,mjs,cjs,js,jsx,json,css,html,yml,yaml}': 'prettier --write',
  '*.md': ['prettier --write', 'markdownlint-cli2 --fix']
};
fs.writeFileSync('package.json', JSON.stringify(p,null,2)+'\n');
"
node -e "const p=require('./package.json'); console.log(JSON.stringify({prepare:p.scripts.prepare, format:p.scripts.format, 'format:check':p.scripts['format:check'], 'lint-staged':p['lint-staged']},null,1));"

# Markdown belongs to markdownlint-cli2, which already has a considered

content.text: Now committing the tooling on its own, so the reformat lands as a separate reviewable commit.

input.command:
git add -A && git status --short && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
build: prettier, lint-staged and husky, with nothing formatted yet

Formatting was a thing everyone did from memory. This adds the tools and
the wiring; the commit after it is the one that actually reformats, kept
separate so this one can be read.

## What runs, and when

`pre-commit` runs lint-staged over the staged files only, so a commit is
formatted without touching work still in the working tree. `pre-push`
asks the pack version question, because CI asks it of a pull request and
two minutes into a workflow run is a bad time to learn that the answer is
a one-line edit. Pushing is also the first moment it is answerable: a
branch is many commits, and asking it of each one fails on every commit
between the first edit and the bump, which teaches you `--no-verify`.

Husky rather than simple-git-hooks, for one reason: the hooks are tracked
files under `.husky/` with `core.hooksPath` pointed at them, so they
arrive with a clone and are visible in review. simple-git-hooks generates
into `.git/hooks`, where nobody can see them and `npm ci --ignore-scripts`
silently skips them. `prepare` activates them on install.

Neither survives `--no-verify`, so CI stays the gate and `format:check`
joins it.

## What the formatter does not touch

**`packs/`.** A pack is a document. Tables are one line per entry so a
d100 reads like the paper it came from. Prettier would explode every
flow-style entry into eight lines of block YAML. Checked that it declines
even when handed a pack file directly, which is how lint-staged passes
them.

**Markdown.** `.markdownlint-cli2.jsonc` already owns docs and already
has the argument written down: one line per paragraph, no fill column,
so a one-word edit does not touch the whole paragraph. Prettier disagrees
with it about emphasis style and table padding both, so it is out, and
lint-staged calls markdownlint on `*.md` instead.

**Comment prose.** Verified rather than assumed: prettier leaves every
doc comment byte-identical.

## The settings that are not defaults

`printWidth: 140`, because this code is written wide: the median line is
35 characters but the 99th percentile is 165, and 80 would be vandalism.

`endOfLine: "auto"`, because the working tree is CRLF. Left at `lf` it
marks 426 of 427 files as needing a change, 135 of them for the line
endings alone.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

content.content:
name: PR title

# The pull request's title becomes the squash commit's title on main, and
# that title decides the version and writes the changelog (see
# CONTRIBUTING.md, "Releases"). So the title is checked here, in
# Conventional Commits form: a type, an optional scope, a short lowercase
# description in the imperative, no period.
#
# pull_request_target rather than pull_request, so the check runs with the
# base repository's token on a fork's pull request too; nothing from the
# pull request is checked out or run, only its title is read.
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, edited, reopened, synchronize]
  # The merge queue asks every required check for a verdict on its merge
  # group. There is no title to check there; the group is made of pull
  # requests that already passed.
  merge_group:

permissions:
  pull-requests: read

jobs:
  title:
    name: Conventional title
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' }}
        uses: amannn/action-semantic-pull-request@v6
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        with:
          types: |
            feat
            fix
            perf
            refactor
            docs
            style
            test
            build
            ci
            chore
            revert
          scopes: |
            run
            designer
            library
            marketplace
            profile
            live
            engine
            schema
            cli
            packs
            hosted
            ci
            docs
            deps
            deps-dev
            release
          requireScope: false
          subjectPattern: ^(?![A-Z]).+(?<!\.)$
          subjectPatternError: |
            The description after the type ("{subject}") should start lowercase, read as an
            instruction ("move the clock under the unit name"), and end without a period.
      - if: ${{ github.event_name == 'merge_group' }}
        run: echo "A merge group has no title to check; its pull requests were checked when they were opened."

content.content:
## Getting set up

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # the app, on localhost
npm test             # the whole suite
npm run typecheck    # all four projects
npm run check:packs  # every shipped pack, --strict
npm run build        # static output in apps/web/dist
```

CI runs the same commands. If they pass locally they pass there.

`.npmrc` asks npm not to install a package version younger than a week, so a compromised release has time to be noticed before it reaches anyone here. npm 11.10 and later enforce it; an older npm ignores the line.

The build knows whether there is anything to sign into from one variable:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `VITE_WORKOS_CLIENT_ID` set | "Sign in" in the header. Set by the deploy from the stage environment's `WORKOS_CLIENT_ID` variable. |
| unset | No sign-in at all, and no request to WorkOS. Local development, the test-suite, a file on disk and the public GitHub Pages build all run this way. |

To work on sign-in locally, put the staging client id in `apps/web/.env.local` and run `npm run dev`; `http://localhost:5173/` is a registered callback. To have an API as well, set `VITE_RUNLOG_API_ORIGIN` there to a hosted Runlog (the dev site, say): the dev server proxies `/api` and `/ws` to it, so live links, widgets by link, sync and purchases work at localhost as they do hosted, against that site's data. `apps/web/.env.example` shows both. Anything else the app talks to has to be named in the Content Security Policy in `hosted/infra/lib/site-stack.ts`, and today that is `api.workos.com` alone.

---

## House style

- **Comments explain why, never what.** The code says what it does. If a comment restates it, delete the comment; if the code needs one to be legible, usually the code should change instead.
- **Name things for the general case.** This began as a companion to one music game and the pull toward its vocabulary is constant. `unit`, `subject`, `run`, never `room`, `track`, `bar`.
- **Report, do not resolve.** Contradictions between rules, disagreements with the environment, honor-system checks: show the player what is in tension and let them rule on it. These games want human judgment, and a tool that silently decides is one people stop trusting.
- **Show the working.** Anything derived (a targeting result especially) carries its derivation, and the UI renders it.

### How it looks

The design has two voices. The pack's author speaks in a book serif, Literata, because the rules are a rulebook. The player speaks in the same face in italic, because a name is a note in the margin. The referee (the app) speaks in IBM Plex Mono, because it keeps a ledger and its figures have to line up. Both faces ship in the bundle: the hosting's Content Security Policy allows no font host, and the worker precaches them like everything else.

Two accents have one job each: celadon is the referee's "fine", kiln amber is consequence. Four looks (lights down, daylight, ember and glaze) share every other decision and differ only in the ground, chosen from the header and remembered on this machine. With no choice made, the operating system's preference picks between the first two.

---

## Checks

A pull request runs the app's checks, the hosting's checks and, where it touches the hosting, a diff of both stages. The merge queue then runs the checks again on main with the queued pull requests merged onto it, which is what will actually land; it does not repeat the diffs, which are for reading. A fork's pull request gets the checks and no diffs, since nothing that reaches AWS runs for it.

The diff is read only where something under `hosted/infra` changed, or the lockfile, or the workflow itself. The site stack names the app build it publishes by its hash, so a pull request that only touches the app still produces a diff, and a diff produced by every pull request is one nobody reads.

The ruleset requires two checks: the pull request's title, and `Checks`, a job that waits for every other check and passes only when they all did (a diff skipped where it is meant to be skipped counts as passed). So a new job, a renamed one or a bigger matrix is a change to the workflow alone; add it to the `needs` of `Checks` and the ruleset follows.

gh pr create --title "build: settle formatting with prettier and run it on commit" --body-file - <<'EOF'
Formatting was a thing everyone did from memory. Three commits, meant to be read in order: the tooling, the reformat, the gate.

## What runs, and when

| Hook | Does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `pre-commit` | lint-staged over the staged files: prettier on code, markdownlint on `*.md` | ~9s on the 298-file reformat commit, well under a second normally |
| `pre-push` | the pack version check, against the merge base with `origin/main` | ~2s |

**Husky rather than simple-git-hooks.** The hooks are tracked files under `.husky/` with `core.hooksPath` pointed at them, so they arrive with a clone and are visible in review; simple-git-hooks generates into `.git/hooks` where nobody can see them and `npm ci --ignore-scripts` silently skips them. npm's `prepare` activates them on install.

**The version check is `pre-push`, not `pre-commit`.** A branch is many commits, and asking it of each one fails on every commit between the first edit and the bump, which teaches you `--no-verify`. Pushing is the first moment it is answerable.

**No hook is a gate.** Each is skipped by `--ignore-scripts`, walked past by `--no-verify`, and absent until somebody installs. So `format:check` joins typecheck and the docs lint in CI, and that is what decides.

## What the formatter does not touch

`.prettierignore` says why at each one.

- **`packs/`** — documents, not code. Tables are one line per entry so a d100 reads like the paper it came from; prettier would explode every flow-style entry into eight lines of block YAML. Checked that it declines even when handed a pack file directly, which is how lint-staged passes them.
- **`*.md`** — markdownlint already owns docs and has the better argument written down in `.markdownlint-cli2.jsonc`: one line per paragraph, no fill column, so a one-word edit does not touch the whole paragraph. Prettier disagrees with it about emphasis style and table padding both.
- **`hosted/pages/`** — templates with `{{PLACEHOLDER}}` substitution, and legal copy a person checks rather than a parser. `hosted.json` is not even valid JSON.
- Generated schema, `docs/reference.md`, `.remember/`.

**Comment prose is untouched.** That was the thing worth checking before running any of this, and it was checked rather than assumed: every doc comment is byte-identical.

## The settings that are not defaults

`printWidth: 140`. This code is written wide — the median line is 35 characters but the 99th percentile is 165 — and 80 would be vandalism. For reference, the churn at each width: 120 → 324 files, 140 → 291, 160 → 261.

`endOfLine: "auto"`. The working tree is CRLF. Left at `lf`, prettier marks 426 of 427 files as needing a change, 135 of them for the line endings alone.

## The reformat

334 files, mechanical, no behaviour in it. Trailing commas added, quotes normalised to double, arguments joined where they fit and split one-per-line where they did not.

`.git-blame-ignore-revs` names that commit so `git blame` attributes a line to the change that made it. GitHub reads the file by name; locally it wants asking once:

```
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
```

## Checks

1160 tests, typecheck, 21 documents validate, 17 fixtures play, `lint:docs` and `format:check` clean — all of it run after the reformat, not before.
EOF

Both PRs are up with auto-merge armed. Summary of where things stand:

## Your three questions

**lint-staged config** — needed one, now in `package.json`: prettier for code, `markdownlint-cli2 --fix` for `*.md`.

**How pre-commit runs** — it didn't, because nothing had installed a hook yet. `simple-git-hooks` would have generated `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, which is why you saw no `.husky/`.

**Contributor propagation** — this is where your instinct was right and my first recommendation was wrong. I'd weighted "lightweight" over "propagates". `simple-git-hooks` writes untracked files into `.git/hooks` that nobody can see in review and `npm ci --ignore-scripts` skips silently. **Switched to husky**: hooks are tracked files in `.husky/`, `core.hooksPath` points at them, `prepare` activates them on `npm install`. They arrive with a clone and are readable in a diff.

Worth saying plainly: no hook manager guarantees anything. `--no-verify` walks past all of them. So `format:check` is now a CI step — the hook is the fast feedback, CI is the gate.

## Two things the measurement changed

**Prettier does not touch comment prose.** I checked rather than assumed, on a comment-heavy file — every doc comment is byte-identical. That was the main risk given how much of this codebase's value is in its comments.

**Markdown is out.** Prettier rewrites your emphasis style (`*backwards*` → `_backwards_`) and pads every table — 98 lines in `authoring.md` alone. `.markdownlint-cli2.jsonc` already owns docs and already argues the case for one line per paragraph. It keeps them.

Also excluded: `packs/` (documents — prettier would explode every flow-style table entry into eight lines of block YAML; I verified it declines even when handed a pack directly, which is how lint-staged passes them), and `hosted/pages/` (`{{PLACEHOLDER}}` templates — `hosted.json` isn't valid JSON, and the legal copy is checked by a person).

`printWidth: 140` because the 99th-percentile line here is 165 characters. `endOfLine: auto` because the tree is CRLF — left at `lf` it flags 426 of 427 files, 135 purely for line endings.

## Also

**#269's title check** was failing on `subjectPattern: ^(?![A-Z]).+(?<!\.)$` — I'd capitalised "Soundclash". Retitled to `fix(packs): ask for platters, not for vinyl`; it passes and the PR is CLEAN.

**No second version bump** on Soundclash: main is at `0.2.0`, the branch at `0.3.0`, so the guard is satisfied. `0.3.0` has never been published, so bumping again would burn a version nobody held — say the word if you'd rather keep the habit anyway.

message.content:
1. Can we add more Elden Ring setups? These should be leveling focused and solely provided resources related to leveling up the player, their weapons, their spirit summons and/or anything else applicable? We should have 1 for each category (e.g. Give Runes, Give Smithing Stones, Give Glovewarts) and possibly one named Give Levels that combines them all?

2. I think we should allow the user to customize the setup further, e.g. with the same Terms customization UI, directly on the run start page. I also think the Setup selection should be a drop-down menu with descriptions included underneath the setup within the menu. The overall UI of the Terms customizer should auto-load the terms specified in the chosen setup/loadout and allow the user to add more, with None defaulting to an empty list. It might also be useful to enable multi-select to combine several loadouts at once. This may cover the final ask on the first item.

content.content:
import { z } from "zod";
import { PackId } from "./primitives.ts";
import type { Diagnostic } from "./lint.ts";

/**
 * A setup: how a run is configured before the first roll.
 *
 * A pack says what the dice can do. A setup says what a tool attached to
 * the game is set to while the run lasts, and what the player is handed
 * to start with: no shields, half damage dealt, fifty thousand runes.
 *
 * It is its own document because it depends on none of the things a pack
 * depends on. The same setup fits every pack for the same game, a mode
 * can name a different one, and one person can write it and everybody
 * else can use it. Held against a pack it would be none of those.
 *
 * What it names is a tool and its operations, which is why it is not part
 * of the pack format: a pack that named `speffect.apply` would be a pack
 * that only plays with one Windows program attached to one game, and the
 * schema has a test against exactly that.
 */

/** One thing to do when a tool attaches. */
export const SetupOp = z
  .object({
    op: z
      .string()
      .min(1)
      .max(64)
      .describe(
        "The operation, in the tool's own vocabulary: `flag.set`, `runes.give`. A tool refuses by name anything its build does not have.",
      ),
    args: z
      .record(z.string(), z.unknown())
      .optional()
      .describe("What the operation takes. Its shape is the tool's business, not this format's."),
    once: z
      .boolean()
      .optional()
      .describe(
        "Given one time in a run rather than every time a tool attaches. The terms go out on every attach, because a tool that restarted is holding none of them and a setting applied twice is the same setting. A gift is not: runes handed over on every reconnect is a different game by the third one.",
      ),
  })
  .strict();

export type SetupOp = z.infer<typeof SetupOp>;

export const Setup = z
  .object({
    kind: z.literal("setup").describe("What this document is. A pack says `pack`; this says `setup`."),
    schemaVersion: z.number().int().positive().describe("The format's major version, as a pack carries one."),
    id: PackId.describe("Reverse-domain id, the way a pack is identified: `com.example.setups.bare-handed`."),
    version: z
      .string()
      .min(1)
      .describe("Semantic version. A setup that changes what it does changes this, or nobody holding it is offered the new one."),
    title: z.string().min(1).max(120).describe("What it is called, on a card and in a chooser."),
    author: z
      .string()
      .max(120)
      .optional()
      .describe("Who wrote it, for a card and a list. A setup travels on its own, so this is the only credit it carries."),
    description: z.string().max(2000).optional().describe("What playing under it is like, in a line or two."),
    /**
     * Which tool this is written for.
     *
     * Operation names say nothing between programs: two tools for two
     * games could both have a `warp.position`, and a setup meant for one
     * of them reaching the other would move somebody for no reason. So a
     * setup names its tool, and anything else listening is sent nothing.
     */
    tool: z.string().min(1).max(64).describe("The tool this is for, by the name that tool calls itself when it attaches."),
    ops: z.array(SetupOp).min(1).max(200).describe("What to do when a tool attaches, in order."),
    license: z
      .object({
        id: z.string().min(1).describe("An SPDX identifier where there is one, else whatever name the terms go by."),
        redistributable: z.boolean().describe("Whether somebody may pass this on. False means it was shared with you, not given to you."),
      })
      .strict()
      .optional()
      .describe("As a pack carries one. Absent means the author said nothing, which is not the same as permission."),
  })
  .strict()
  .describe(
    "What a tool attached to the game is set to while a run lasts, and what the player is handed " +
      "to start with. Written for a tool rather than for a pack, so one fits every pack for the same game.",
  );

export type Setup = z.infer<typeof Setup>;

export type SetupResult = { ok: true; setup: Setup; diagnostics: Diagnostic[] } | { ok: false; setup: null; diagnostics: Diagnostic[] };

/** The major version of this format that this build understands. */
export const SETUP_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1;

 * Validate an untrusted object into a Setup.
 *
 * Two gates rather than the pack's three: a version, and a shape. There
 * is no coherence pass because there is nothing here to be incoherent

content.text:
I have what I need. Both asks are clear; the second one is bigger than it looks.

## 1. The setups — straightforward

Exact item names pulled from the tool's own list (`apps/web/src/control/lists/tarnishedtool.json`), not from memory. Two I'd have got wrong: `Great Grave Glovewort` / `Great Ghost Glovewort` (the +9→+10 materials) and `Somber Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone`.

| Setup | What it hands over |
|---|---|
| **Give Runes** | `runes.give`, one lump |
| **Give Smithing Stones** | Smithing Stone [1]–[8], Somber [1]–[9], both Ancient Dragon stones |
| **Give Gloveworts** | Grave [1]–[9], Ghost [1]–[9], Great Grave, Great Ghost |
| **Give Flask Upgrades** | Golden Seed, Sacred Tear |
| **Give Larval Tears** | `Larval Tear (Base Game)` — the tool splits base/DLC |
| **Give Memory Stones** | Memory Stone |
| **Give Scadutree Blessings** | Scadutree Fragment, Revered Spirit Ash (DLC) |

`item.named` caps `quantity` at 99 per line, so each material is one op at 99. All ops get `once: true` — the schema is explicit that a gift re-applied on every reconnect is a different game by the third one.

Two notes. These are *utilities*, so your `Give X` naming is right even though the existing seven are evocative (`Cleric`, `Glass`, `Long night`) — different kind of document, different naming. And I'd **skip "Give Levels"**: multi-select makes it redundant the day it lands, and it's one file to add later if you want it sooner.

## 2. The run-start customizer — three things worth deciding before I build

**A native `<select>` can't do what you're describing.** It can't render a description under each option, and `<select multiple>` is genuinely bad UX. What you're actually describing — title plus description per row, several of them selectable — is a checkbox list, which is *what the page already has* (`.choice` cards with title + description); the change is multi-select, plus collapsing it behind a disclosure (`Setup: None ▾`) so it doesn't dominate the start page. Same compactness, keeps the descriptions.

**The stored shape has to go plural.** Today a run keeps one `ChosenSetup { id, version, title, ops }` with ops copied. Combining and editing needs:

```ts
interface ChosenSetup {
  from: Array<{ id; version; title }>;   // provenance: "played under Cleric and Give Runes"
  ops: ProfileOp[];                      // what actually gets sent, edited or not
}
```

`chosenFrom` must keep reading the old single-setup shape — people have runs on their devices right now. That's a hard requirement, not a nicety.

**Editing makes "played under Cleric" a lie.** Once the ops are yours, the run's record should say *seeded from* Cleric and Give Runes, *then edited* — otherwise a log that sells itself on honesty is quietly wrong. Cheap to do, easy to forget.

One thing that falls out nicely: combining setups can conflict (two that both `value.set player.vigor` — last wins; two that both `runes.give` — both apply). Because the merged list lands in the editable Ops list, **you see the conflict and can delete a line**, rather than it being resolved invisibly. I'd keep the pack author's terms (`profile.setup`) separate from the player's, as `withChosen` does now, or the author's half gets clobbered.

`Ops` currently lives inside `ControlSettings.tsx`; it's already self-contained (`catalog`, `lists`, `ops`, `onChange`), so extracting it to its own module for reuse is clean.

python - <<'PY'
import io, os

HEAD = """# yaml-language-server: $schema=../../packages/rules-schema/schema/setup-1.schema.json

kind: setup
schemaVersion: 1
id: com.scrthq.runlog.setups.{slug}
version: "1.0.0"
title: {title}
author: Runlog
description: >-
{desc}

tool: TarnishedTool

ops:
{ops}

license:
  id: MIT
  redistributable: true
"""

def item(name, qty=99):
    return '  - { op: item.named, args: { name: %s, quantity: %d }, once: true }' % (
        ('"%s"' % name) if any(c in name for c in "[](),:") else name, qty)

def wrap(text, indent="  "):
    words, lines, cur = text.split(), [], indent
    for w in words:
        if len(cur) + len(w) + 1 > 74:
            lines.append(cur.rstrip()); cur = indent
        cur += w + " "
    lines.append(cur.rstrip())
    return "\n".join(lines)

setups = []

setups.append(("give-runes", "Give Runes", """
# Levels, bought rather than earned.
#
# One lump, once. `runes.give` adds and cannot set, because nothing in
# the game says how many somebody is carrying, so there is no number to
# set one to; and it is `once` because a gift re-applied on every
# reconnect is a different game by the third one.
""".strip(),
 "Ten million runes, handed over once. Enough to level to wherever you meant to start, and to buy the things you would have gone shopping for.",
 ['  - { op: runes.give, args: { amount: 10000000 }, once: true }']))

smith = [item("Smithing Stone [%d]" % i) for i in range(1, 9)]
smith += [item("Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone")]
smith += [item("Somber Smithing Stone [%d]" % i) for i in range(1, 10)]
smith += [item("Somber Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone")]
setups.append(("give-smithing-stones", "Give Smithing Stones", """
# Every weapon to its ceiling, without the mining.
#
# Ordinary stones take a weapon to +25 and somber ones to +10; the two
# Ancient Dragon stones are the last step of each. Ninety-nine of each
# is the most one operation may hand over, and it is more than a run
# will get through.
""".strip(),
 "Ninety-nine of every smithing stone, ordinary and somber, up to and including both Ancient Dragon stones. Any weapon, to any level, whenever you feel like it.",
 smith))

glove = [item("Grave Glovewort [%d]" % i) for i in range(1, 10)]
glove += [item("Great Grave Glovewort")]
glove += [item("Ghost Glovewort [%d]" % i) for i in range(1, 10)]
glove += [item("Great Ghost Glovewort")]
setups.append(("give-gloveworts", "Give Gloveworts", """
# The spirits, brought up to where the player is.
#
# Grave glovewort upgrades an ordinary ash and ghost glovewort a `+`
# one; the two Great ones are the last step of each. A summon left at
# the level it was found at is the usual reason a summon stops being
# worth calling.
""".strip(),
 "Ninety-nine of every glovewort, grave and ghost, including both Great ones. Every spirit ash you own can go to its ceiling.",
 glove))

setups.append(("give-flask-upgrades", "Give Flask Upgrades", """
# The flask, at full.
#
# Golden seeds add charges and sacred tears make each charge worth
# more. Both are the ordinary reason an early-game run cannot survive a
# late-game fight, and neither is interesting to go and find again.
""".strip(),
 "Golden seeds and sacred tears, enough of each to take the flask as far as it goes. More charges, and more in every charge.",
 [item("Golden Seed", 99), item("Sacred Tear", 99)]))

setups.append(("give-larval-tears", "Give Larval Tears", """
# Respec, as often as you like.
#
# The tool lists the base game's tear and the DLC's separately, because
# they are separate items. This hands over the base game's, which is
# the one Rennala asks for.
""".strip(),
 "Ninety-nine larval tears. Rebuild the character as often as the run makes you want to, without going to look for one first.",
 [item("Larval Tear (Base Game)", 99)]))

setups.append(("give-memory-stones", "Give Memory Stones", """
# Somewhere to put the spells.
#
# A memory stone is a spell slot. A caster who has found none is a
# caster with two spells, which is a different game from the one a
# sorcery run is trying to be.
""".strip(),
 "Ninety-nine memory stones, so every spell you own has somewhere to sit. For a run that means to cast rather than to go looking for slots.",
 [item("Memory Stone", 99)]))

setups.append(("give-scadutree-blessings", "Give Scadutree Blessings", """
# The DLC's own levelling, which the player's level does not touch.
#
# Shadow of the Erdtree scales damage taken and dealt by two counts of
# its own: scadutree fragments for the player, revered spirit ash for
# the summons. A run that enters at level two hundred and ignores these
# is still a run that dies in one hit.
""".strip(),
 "Scadutree fragments and revered spirit ash, the DLC's own levelling for the player and for their summons. Needed by any run that goes into Shadow of the Erdtree.",
 [item("Scadutree Fragment", 99), item("Revered Spirit Ash", 99)]))

for slug, title, banner, desc, ops in setups:
    body = banner + "\n\n" + HEAD.format(slug=slug, title=title, desc=wrap(desc), ops="\n".join(ops))
    path = "packs/setups/elden-ring-%s.yaml" % slug
    open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n").write(body)
    print("wrote", path, "-", len(ops), "ops")
PY

 * than each doing the conversion its own way.

"""Build Elden Ring: TarnishedTool's states, tables and control profile
from one source.

Run it from anywhere: python packs/profiles/build-tarnishedtool.py


Each curse row is (weight, id, text, state, ops). `state` is
(id, label, short, description) or None; `ops` is what a tool does about
it, or None for a vow that only the player enforces.
"""
import io, json, os, re, textwrap

def wrap(text, indent):
    return [" " * indent + l for l in textwrap.wrap(text, 68 - indent)]

def flag(name, value=True):
    return [{"op": "flag.set", "args": {"name": name, "value": value}}]

def val(name, v):
    return [{"op": "value.set", "args": {"name": name, "value": v}}]

def runes(amount):
    """Runes given or taken. Not a number anything can read, so it adds."""
    return [{"op": "runes.give", "args": {"amount": amount}}]

def press(action):
    return [{"op": "action.invoke", "args": {"action": action}}]

def watch_boss(name=None, area=None):
    """Say when a boss dies. No name means any of them."""

import re, os

def q(path, pairs, desc=None, banner=None):
    p = "packs/setups/elden-ring-%s.yaml" % path
    s = open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()
    for pat, qty in pairs:
        s = re.sub(r'(name: %s, quantity: )\d+' % re.escape(pat), r'\g<1>%d' % qty, s)
    if desc:
        s = re.sub(r'description: >-\n(?:  .*\n)+', desc, s)
    if banner:
        s = re.sub(r'\A(?:#.*\n)+', banner, s)
    open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n").write(s)

# Smithing: an ordinary weapon eats several stones a level, a somber one exactly one.
for i in range(1, 9):
    q("give-smithing-stones", [('"Smithing Stone [%d]"' % i, 20)])
for i in range(1, 10):
    q("give-smithing-stones", [('"Somber Smithing Stone [%d]"' % i, 8)])
q("give-smithing-stones", [("Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone", 8), ("Somber Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone", 4)],
  desc="description: >-\n  Enough of every smithing stone to take a couple of ordinary weapons to\n  the top and a handful of somber ones with them. Ordinary stones go\n  twenty to a tier because an ordinary weapon eats several a level;\n  somber ones go eight, because a somber weapon eats exactly one.\n",
  banner="# Weapons, taken most of the way, without the mining.\n#\n# The amounts are a boost rather than a shopping trip: enough to stop\n# the run being about materials, not so much that nothing is worth\n# picking up. An ordinary weapon takes several stones a level and a\n# somber one takes exactly one, which is why the two tiers differ.\n")

for i in range(1, 10):
    q("give-gloveworts", [('"Grave Glovewort [%d]"' % i, 10), ('"Ghost Glovewort [%d]"' % i, 10)])
q("give-gloveworts", [("Great Grave Glovewort", 5), ("Great Ghost Glovewort", 5)],
  desc="description: >-\n  Ten of every glovewort, grave and ghost, and five of each Great one.\n  Enough to bring several spirit ashes up to where the player is,\n  rather than enough to never think about one again.\n",
  banner="# The spirits, brought up to where the player is.\n#\n# Grave glovewort upgrades an ordinary ash and ghost glovewort a `+`\n# one; the two Great ones are the last step of each. Ten a tier is\n# several summons raised, which is the boost; it is deliberately not so\n# many that a glovewort on the ground stops being worth bending for.\n")

q("give-flask-upgrades", [("Golden Seed", 20), ("Sacred Tear", 10)],
  desc="description: >-\n  Twenty golden seeds and ten sacred tears: a great many more charges,\n  and a great deal more in each of them. Enough that the flask stops\n  being the reason a run ends early.\n")

q("give-larval-tears", [("Larval Tear (Base Game)", 10)],
  desc="description: >-\n  Ten larval tears. Rebuild the character when the run makes you want\n  to, without going to look for one first, and without the number\n  being so large that the choice stops costing anything.\n")

q("give-memory-stones", [("Memory Stone", 8)],
  desc="description: >-\n  Eight memory stones, so the spells you own have somewhere to sit. For\n  a run that means to cast, rather than to go looking for slots first.\n")

q("give-scadutree-blessings", [("Scadutree Fragment", 20), ("Revered Spirit Ash", 15)],
  desc="description: >-\n  Twenty scadutree fragments and fifteen revered spirit ash: the DLC's\n  own levelling for the player and for their summons, well up from\n  nothing. Worth having for any run that goes into Shadow of the Erdtree.\n")

# Runes: an order of magnitude above the loadouts that already give some,
# rather than a number with no relationship to them.
p = "packs/setups/elden-ring-give-runes.yaml"
s = open(p, encoding="utf-8").read()
s = s.replace("amount: 10000000", "amount: 1000000")
s = re.sub(r'description: >-\n(?:  .*\n)+',
  "description: >-\n  A million runes, handed over once. Enough to level well past where the\n  run would have started you and to buy what you would have gone\n  shopping for, without being so much that spending stops mattering.\n", s)
open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n").write(s)
print("done")
PY

git add packs/setups/ package.json apps/web/src/control/setups.test.ts && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(packs): seven Elden Ring loadouts that hand over the materials

The seven that shipped say who you are: a cleric, a brute, a sorcerer.
None of them say what you are made of. A run that means to use a weapon
it found still has to go and mine for it, and the mining is not the game
anybody sat down to play.

| Loadout | Hands over |
|---|---|
| Give Runes | A million, once |
| Give Smithing Stones | Every tier, ordinary and somber, both Ancient Dragon stones |
| Give Gloveworts | Grave and ghost, every tier, both Great ones |
| Give Flask Upgrades | Golden seeds and sacred tears |
| Give Larval Tears | Ten respecs |
| Give Memory Stones | Eight spell slots |
| Give Scadutree Blessings | The DLC's own leveling, for the player and their summons |

The amounts are a generous boost rather than a shopping trip: twenty of
an ordinary smithing stone a tier and eight of a somber one, because an
ordinary weapon eats several a level and a somber one eats exactly one.
Enough that materials stop being what the run is about, not so much that
a glovewort on the ground stops being worth bending for.

Every one is `once`. A gift handed over again on every reconnect is a
different game by the third one, which is what the flag is for.

## A guard, because this is the failure that says nothing

`item.named` takes a string, and the format deliberately says nothing
about what may be in it: the shape of an operation's arguments is the
tool's business, which is what lets one format serve tools nobody here
has heard of. The cost is that a misspelling validates, ships, and then
quietly hands over nothing, on the one screen where nobody is looking at
the app to find out.

The lists the tool publishes are already in this repository, for the
pickers in Settings. So the setups are now held against them, and the
test fails with the name it could not find. It caught two I would have
got wrong from memory while writing these: the +9 materials are **Great**
Grave and Ghost Glovewort, and the somber capstone is **Somber Ancient
Dragon Smithing Stone**, not the other order.

87 names across every shipped setup check out.
EOF

it found still has to go and mine for it, and the mining is not the game
anybody sat down to play.

| Loadout | Hands over |
|---|---|
| Give Runes | A million, once |
| Give Smithing Stones | Every tier, ordinary and somber, both Ancient Dragon stones |
| Give Gloveworts | Grave and ghost, every tier, both Great ones |
| Give Flask Upgrades | Golden seeds and sacred tears |
| Give Larval Tears | Ten respecs |
| Give Memory Stones | Eight spell slots |
| Give Scadutree Blessings | The DLC's own leveling, for the player and their summons |

The amounts are a generous boost rather than a shopping trip: twenty of
an ordinary smithing stone a tier and eight of a somber one, because an
ordinary weapon eats several a level and a somber one eats exactly one.
Enough that materials stop being what the run is about, not so much that
a glovewort on the ground stops being worth bending for.

Every one is `once`. A gift handed over again on every reconnect is a
different game by the third one, which is what the flag is for.

## A guard, because this is the failure that says nothing

`item.named` takes a string, and the format deliberately says nothing
about what may be in it: the shape of an operation's arguments is the
tool's business, which is what lets one format serve tools nobody here
has heard of. The cost is that a misspelling validates, ships, and then
quietly hands over nothing, on the one screen where nobody is looking at
the app to find out.

The lists the tool publishes are already in this repository, for the
pickers in Settings. So the setups are now held against them, and the
test fails with the name it could not find. It caught two I would have
got wrong from memory while writing these: the +9 materials are **Great**
Grave and Ghost Glovewort, and the somber capstone is **Somber Ancient
Dragon Smithing Stone**, not the other order.

87 names across every shipped setup check out.

feat(run): choose several loadouts, and change what they hand over

A loadout was one choice out of a list, taken or not. Two things were
wrong with that. "A knight's armor" and "enough stones to use it" are
two sentences and wanting both is the ordinary case; and a loadout that
is almost right is far more common than one that is exactly right, so
the usual repair was to start the run and then go and fix it in
Settings.

Now the list is ticked rather than picked, what the ticked ones hand
over is shown as a list, and that list is the editor Settings already
used for a run's terms.

## What a run keeps

`ChosenSetup` was `{ id, version, title, ops }`. It is now:

```ts
{ from: [{ id, version, title }], ops, edited? }
```

Three fields answering three questions. `ops` is what gets sent, which
is all the tool cares about. `from` is where it came from. `edited` is
whether it is still what those loadouts said.

That last one earns its place. "Played under Cleric" is a fact until the
operations are editable and a claim afterwards, and a log that sells
itself on being an honest record should not make claims it cannot check.
So the screen says **"Seeded from Well armed and Give Smithing Stones,
then edited"** the moment a line is removed. The flag is computed rather
than set, because an editor that had to remember would one day forget.

still understood and reads as a run seeded from that one loadout, which
is what it was. People have runs open on their devices right now.

## What is deliberately not done

Nothing is merged or de-duplicated. Two loadouts that set the same value
leave both lines in and the last wins, which is what a tool would do
anyway; two that give runes give both lots. Resolving that quietly would
be the wrong favor, because the list is in front of the player and a
line they did not want is a line they can delete.

`Ops` and `Arg` move out of `ControlSettings.tsx` into `Ops.tsx`,
unchanged, because two screens need them now.

lot on a page that also has a mode, a seed, a name and the requirements.
With nothing chosen that button says "Choose a Loadout" rather than
"None" — a button reading "None" is a statement, not an invitation, and
folding the list must not hide that there is a list.

1175 tests. Driven in the browser: two loadouts combine to 32 operations,
deleting one flips the credit line, and emptying the list keeps the
credit honest rather than pretending nothing was chosen.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\xbox\.claude\plugins\cache\deslop-text\deslop-text\1441f2267525\skills\deslop-text

You are reviewing written text for AI-generated writing patterns. These are the word choices, sentence constructions, and structural habits that make text immediately recognisable as machine-generated. The goal is text that reads as if a specific human wrote it with a specific point to make.

## How to run this review

1. Identify the target. If the user specified a file, read it. If they pasted text, use that. If neither, ask.
2. Run every check in the **30 warning signs** below against the text.
3. For each violation found, cite the specific phrase or sentence and state which warning sign it triggers.
4. Suggest a concrete rewrite for each violation. Do not just say "remove this" — show what the sentence becomes.
5. Report findings grouped by severity:
   - **High** — patterns that are instant AI tells (W1 filler phrases, W5 marketing language, W6 generic openings, W9 paired adjectives, W15 excited-to-announce)
   - **Medium** — patterns that weaken the writing even when not obviously AI (W3 em-dashes, W7 passive voice, W8 hedging, W11 mechanical transitions, W26 uncontracted forms)
   - **Low** — statistical patterns that only matter in aggregate (W20 "very", W28 repetitive words, W29 sentence length uniformity)
6. End with a count: "X violations found across Y of 32 checks."
7. If the user asks you to fix the text (not just review), apply all rewrites and present the cleaned version.

---

## The 32 warning signs

### W1 · Filler phrases

Phrases that add no meaning. Delete them or rewrite the sentence without them.

Target phrases:
- "it's worth noting", "it bears mentioning", "it goes without saying"
- "at the end of the day", "moving forward", "when all is said and done"
- "delve into", "navigate" (used metaphorically), "underscore" (as emphasis verb)
- "leverage" (as a verb), "utilize" (instead of "use")
- "nuanced", "tapestry", "landscape" (used metaphorically)
- "not only X but also Y"
- "holistic", "robust", "cutting-edge"

### W2 · "Not X, it is Y" constructions

Contrastive framing where the negation adds nothing. The positive statement carries the meaning; the negation is just runway.

The pattern takes many forms:
- Single sentence: "This is not about speed, it is about reliability."
- Split across sentences: "It's not about speed. It's about reliability."
- Inverted/rhetorical: "Speed? No. Reliability."
- With contractions: "It's not one big giveaway. It's a pile of small ones."
- Softer forms: "less about X, more about Y"

Flag any adjacent sentence pair where one negates and the next affirms the same subject, regardless of exact phrasing.

Fix: say what it is directly. Cut the negation.

### W3 · Em-dash overuse

Dashes bolting parenthetical asides onto sentences. One em-dash per document is fine. Three or more is a pattern.

Flag if: more than one dash-delimited aside per paragraph, or more than 3 em-dashes in the full document.

Fix: if the aside matters, give it its own sentence. If not, cut it.

### W4 · Rhetorical questions

Questions used as section openers or transitions rather than genuine inquiry. "What if you could automate your entire workflow?"

Flag if: more than one rhetorical question per 500 words.

Exception: do NOT flag "Question? Answer." pairs where the sentence immediately following the question is a direct answer to it. This is intentional structure (e.g., "How did we solve this? We built a simulator."). Only flag rhetorical questions that are standalone openers or transitions with no direct answer following.

Fix: merge the question and answer into a single declarative sentence, or convert to a "To [verb]..." construction. Never delete just the question and leave the answer orphaned as a non-sequitur statement.

### W5 · Marketing language

Adjectives that sell rather than describe.

Target words: "powerful", "seamless", "revolutionary", "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "best-in-class", "world-class", "next-generation", "innovative", "groundbreaking", "transformative".

Fix: replace with a specific, factual description. "Powerful search" becomes "search that handles 10M records in under 200ms."

### W6 · Generic openings

Opening sentences that could begin any article on any topic.

Target patterns:
- "In today's [connected/digital/fast-paced/modern] world..."
- "As we all know..."
- "Have you ever wondered..."
- "Imagine [a world where/if you could]..."
- "[Industry] is evolving rapidly..."

Fix: start with the specific claim, finding, or situation.

### W7 · Passive voice as habit

Consistent use of passive constructions where active voice would be clearer.

Look for: "was [verb]ed", "is being [verb]ed", "has been [verb]ed", "it was found", "it was determined", "it can be seen".

Flag if: passive constructions exceed 20% of sentences.

Fix: name the actor. "It was found that..." becomes "We found..."

### W8 · Excessive hedging

Qualifying every statement into meaninglessness.

Target patterns: "it seems like", "it appears that", "it could be argued", "one might say", "it is possible that", "arguably", "perhaps", "in some ways".

Flag if: more than 2 hedging phrases per 500 words.

Fix: commit to the claim or cut the sentence.

### W9 · Paired adjectives with "yet" or "and"

"Simple yet powerful", "elegant and robust", "lightweight but comprehensive".

Fix: pick the stronger adjective. Drop the pairing.

### W10 · Meta-references

Text that narrates its own structure instead of just having structure.

Third-person/impersonal forms: "In this post...", "As we discussed above...", "Let's explore...", "In this article...", "As mentioned earlier...", "Below, we'll cover..."

First-person forms: "I grouped them into three tiers based on...", "I've organized these by...", "I read through this list and realized...", "I want to walk you through..."

Both do the same thing: tell the reader about the article's organization rather than letting the organization speak for itself.

Fix: delete. The reader knows they are reading the post. If the structure is clear, you don't need to announce it.

### W11 · Mechanical transitions

Formulaic transition words used to connect paragraphs.

Target: "Furthermore", "Moreover", "Additionally", "In conclusion", "That said", "With that in mind", "Having established that", "It is also worth mentioning".

Fix: connect ideas with a sentence that earns the transition, or just start the next paragraph without one.

### W12 · Bold emphasis in body copy

`<strong>` or `<b>` wrapping a short phrase inside a paragraph to highlight a key selling point: "with **zero configuration**", "in **days rather than months**".

Flag if: 2+ paragraphs use this, or 1 instance appears in the hero subheadline.

Fix: rewrite so emphasis comes from sentence position. Or give the phrase its own line.

### W13 · Scare quotes

Quotation marks used for emphasis or irony around ordinary words, not actual quotations. The tool "seamlessly" integrates.

Fix: choose a better word. Drop the quotes.

### W14 · Section-end summaries

Closing a section by restating what was just said. The last sentence of a section paraphrases the first sentence or heading.

Fix: delete. Move on.

### W15 · "Excited to announce/share" openers

"We're excited to announce...", "I'm thrilled to share...", "We're proud to present...".

Fix: state what happened. "We shipped X" not "We're excited to announce X."

### W16 · "Whether you're X or Y" false inclusivity

"Whether you're a startup founder or an enterprise CTO...", "Whether you're just getting started or scaling to millions..."

Fix: pick the actual audience and speak to them directly.

### W17 · Faux-conversational pivots

"Here's the thing:", "Let me be clear:", "The truth is:", "Look:", "So here's what happened:".

Fix: delete the pivot. Start with the substance.

### W18 · Exclamation mark clusters

Multiple exclamation marks in close proximity.

Flag if: more than 1 in any paragraph, or more than 3 in the full document.

Fix: remove all but the one that matters most.

### W19 · Repetitive "You" sentence starters

Multiple consecutive sentences or paragraphs starting with "You".

Flag if: 3+ consecutive sentences begin with "You".

Fix: vary sentence structure. Lead with the action, result, or situation.

### W20 · The word "very"

"Very" weakens specificity. "Very fast" is less precise than "fast" or a specific measurement.

Fix: delete "very" or replace with a specific descriptor.

### W21 · Corporate cliches

Phrases that sound authoritative but say nothing specific.

Target: "think outside the box", "move the needle", "growth mindset", "digital transformation", "synergy", "ecosystem", "paradigm shift", "disruptive", "thought leader", "best practices", "deep dive" (as a noun), "double down", "circle back", "take it to the next level", "game changer", "mission-critical".

Fix: replace with a specific, concrete statement.

### W22 · Hashtag blocks

Blocks of 2+ `#CamelCase` hashtags appended to text.

Fix: delete the hashtag block.

### W23 · Emoji as emphasis

Clusters of decorative emoji (rocket, fire, sparkle, lightbulb, star, checkmark, pointing finger) used for energy in marketing text.

Flag if: 2+ emphasis emoji appear.

Fix: delete the emoji. Let the words carry the weight.

### W24 · Triple-value lists

Three abstract virtues listed in "X, Y, and Z" form: "excellence, collaboration, and innovation". Sounds principled, says nothing concrete.

Fix: pick the one that matters and say something specific about it.

### W25 · Informal corporate slang

Metaphorical business jargon: "circle back", "low-hanging fruit", "boil the ocean", "bandwidth" (used metaphorically), "deep dive", "touch base", "move the needle", "table this", "unpack this", "lean into".

Fix: say what you mean in plain language.

### W26 · Uncontracted forms

"It is", "do not", "is not", "we are", "they have" used consistently with zero contractions anywhere. Produces stiff, formal prose.

Flag if: 2+ uncontracted forms exist and no contractions appear in the entire text.

Fix: use contractions. "It is" becomes "it's", "do not" becomes "don't".

### W27 · Typographic quotes

Curly/smart quotes and smart apostrophes instead of straight quotes. Keyboards produce straight quotes; AI models often output curly ones.

Fix: replace curly quotes with straight quotes.

### W28 · Repetitive word use

Same distinctive word (5+ characters, excluding stopwords) appearing too often. Check two levels:

- **Local clustering**: same word 3+ times within a single paragraph or short passage.
- **Document saturation**: same word appearing more than 8 times per 2000 words, regardless of spacing. A word can pass every local check while still dominating the piece.

Fix: use a synonym, restructure, or cut redundant sentences. For document-level saturation, the fix is often that the text is making the same point repeatedly (see also W31).

### W29 · Sentence length uniformity

4+ consecutive sentences all within 30% of their mean word count. AI tends to produce metronomic sentence lengths; real writing varies.

Fix: vary sentence length. Mix short and long. A three-word sentence after a complex one creates rhythm.

### W30 · Heading emoji

Decorative emoji at the start of markdown headings: "## Getting Started", "### Key Takeaways".

Fix: remove the emoji from the heading.

### W31 · Repeated thematic points

The same idea restated in different words at multiple points in the text. AI tends to re-derive its thesis in every section, producing multiple phrasings of one point rather than advancing the argument.

Example — these three sentences from different sections all say the same thing:
- "Each pattern is individually forgivable. Stacked together, they're a fingerprint."
- "These don't scream AI on their own... they pile up into a recognizable texture."
- "Any single instance means nothing. But when you see all of them, something feels off."

Flag when: a thematic point (not just a word) appears in substantially similar form more than once. Pay attention to the "[one/single/individual] is [fine/nothing]. [Together/combined/stacked] they [signal/reveal]" structure, but don't limit detection to that template.

Fix: say it once, in the strongest place. Delete or replace the weaker instances with points that advance the argument.

### W32 · Internet cliches

Phrases that were novel online circa 2015-2022 but have been strip-mined by AI models into cliche. They aren't corporate jargon (W21) or filler (W1) — they're internet-native expressions that AI reaches for as if they're still fresh.

Target phrases:
- "you can't unsee it/them"
- "hits different"
- "rent-free"
- "chef's kiss"
- "the quiet part out loud"
- "I'm here for it"
- "tell me you X without telling me you X"
- "let that sink in"
- "this is the way"
- "say it louder for the people in the back"

Fix: say what you actually mean. If the phrase is doing real work, replace it with a specific observation. If it's decoration, delete it.

---

## Severity classification

**High** (instant AI tells — fix these first):
W1 (filler phrases), W2 ("not X, it is Y"), W5 (marketing language), W6 (generic openings), W9 (paired adjectives), W15 (excited-to-announce), W16 (whether you're X or Y), W17 (faux-conversational pivots), W21 (corporate cliches), W24 (triple-value lists)

**Medium** (weaken the writing):
W3 (em-dashes), W4 (rhetorical questions), W7 (passive voice), W8 (hedging), W10 (meta-references), W11 (mechanical transitions), W12 (bold emphasis), W13 (scare quotes), W14 (section-end summaries), W18 (exclamation clusters), W19 (repetitive "You"), W22 (hashtags), W23 (emoji), W25 (corporate slang), W26 (uncontracted forms), W30 (heading emoji), W32 (internet cliches)

**Low** (statistical — matter in aggregate):
W20 ("very"), W27 (typographic quotes), W28 (repetitive words), W29 (sentence length uniformity), W31 (repeated thematic points)

---

## Principles

- Every rewrite must preserve the original meaning. Removing slop is not an excuse to change what the text says.
- When fixing W5 (marketing language), the replacement must be specific and factual. "Powerful" cannot just become "strong" — it must become a concrete claim.
- When fixing W2 ("not X, it is Y"), keep the Y. The positive statement is almost always the one that matters.
- When multiple violations overlap in one sentence, rewrite the whole sentence once rather than fixing each pattern individually.
- A clean text is not a bland text. The goal is writing with a specific voice and specific claims, not writing with all personality removed.

Two asks, and the second one turned out to cover the tail of the first.

## Seven loadouts that hand over materials

The seven that shipped say *who you are* — a cleric, a brute, a sorcerer. None say what you are made of, so a run that means to use a weapon it found still has to go and mine for it.

| Loadout | Hands over |
|---|---|
| Give Runes | A million, once |
| Give Smithing Stones | Every tier, ordinary and somber, both Ancient Dragon stones |
| Give Gloveworts | Grave and ghost, every tier, both Great ones |
| Give Flask Upgrades | Golden seeds and sacred tears |
| Give Larval Tears | Ten respecs |
| Give Memory Stones | Eight spell slots |
| Give Scadutree Blessings | The DLC's own leveling, for the player and their summons |

Amounts are a generous boost rather than a shopping trip: twenty of an ordinary smithing stone a tier, eight of a somber one, because an ordinary weapon eats several a level and a somber one eats exactly one. Every op is `once` — a gift re-applied on every reconnect is a different game by the third one.

**No "Give Levels".** Multi-select makes it redundant.

### A guard for the failure that says nothing

`item.named` takes a string and the format says nothing about what may be in it — the shape of an operation's arguments is the tool's business, which is what lets one format serve tools nobody here has heard of. The cost is that a misspelling validates, ships, and then quietly hands over nothing.

The tool's own lists are already in the repo for the pickers in Settings, so the shipped setups are held against them now. It caught two I had wrong from memory: the +9 materials are **Great** Grave/Ghost Glovewort, and the capstone is **Somber Ancient Dragon Smithing Stone**. 87 names check out.

## Choosing several, and changing what they hand over

`ChosenSetup` was `{ id, version, title, ops }`. Now:

```ts
{ from: [{ id, version, title }], ops, edited? }
```

`ops` is what gets sent. `from` is where it came from. `edited` is whether it is still what those loadouts said — because "Played under Cleric" is a fact until the operations are editable and a claim afterwards, and a log that sells itself on being an honest record should not make claims it cannot check. The screen says **"Seeded from Well armed and Give Smithing Stones, then edited"** the moment a line goes. The flag is computed, so an editor cannot forget to set it.

**Runs written before this are read.** The old single-setup shape reads as a run seeded from that one loadout. People have runs open right now.

Nothing is merged or de-duplicated. Two loadouts that set the same value leave both lines in and the last wins; two that give runes give both lots. The list is in front of you and a line you did not want is one you can delete.

`Ops` and `Arg` move out of `ControlSettings.tsx` into `Ops.tsx`, unchanged, because two screens need them.

## The UI, after using it

The first pass was a disclosure, not a menu — fourteen cards in a three-column grid that pushed the whole form down. It is a menu now: floats, scrolls at 22rem, closes on Escape or an outside press. Rows, not cards.

The editor is always there, including under "None", as an empty list with **Add custom loadout** — otherwise there is no way to write terms without picking a loadout and then emptying it.

Layout: fields sized by what they hold (a weapon's level is 0–25 and was seven rem wide), the op select capped, remove buttons pinned to a single right edge, rows that do not wrap.

**One thing does not fit and cannot.** A weapon row is five controls; its two longest names still overflow by a few pixels. Every other row in every shipped loadout is clean. The alternatives are wrapping the row or clipping the select, both worse.

## Also

American spellings the September sweep missed — six, all in comments. `cancelled()` stays, being GitHub's own function.

## Checks

1176 tests, typecheck, 28 documents validate, `lint:docs` and `format:check` clean. Driven in the browser across all 14 loadouts at 77 rows: no wrapping, buttons aligned, one field short.
EOF

content.text:
[PR #271](https://github.com/SCRT-HQ/runlog/pull/271) is up with auto-merge armed. The only uncommitted thing is `.entire/`, left untracked deliberately — see the note at the end.

## The seven loadouts

`Give Runes`, `Give Smithing Stones`, `Give Gloveworts`, `Give Flask Upgrades`, `Give Larval Tears`, `Give Memory Stones`, `Give Scadutree Blessings`. Quantities are a boost, not a shopping trip, per your note — twenty of an ordinary smithing stone a tier, eight of a somber one, since an ordinary weapon eats several a level and a somber one eats exactly one.

I skipped "Give Levels" — multi-select makes it redundant, as you predicted.

**Talisman pouches aren't possible.** TarnishedTool has no way to grant one: not in its 1,644 items, not a `value.set` name, not an invokable action. The only capacity items it exposes are `Memory Stone` and `Stone of Gurranq`. The lists are generated from the tool's own resources, so this isn't a stale copy — the operation doesn't exist. If the tool gains one, the setup is a four-line file.

I also added a guard that holds every shipped setup's item names against those lists, because a misspelling validates, ships, and then silently hands over nothing. It caught two I'd have got wrong from memory: **Great** Grave/Ghost Glovewort, and **Somber Ancient Dragon** Smithing Stone.

## The picker

Multi-select, a real floating menu, and the ops editor seeded from whatever you tick — editable, and present under "None" as an empty list with **Add custom loadout**.

The one design call worth flagging: once the ops are editable, "Played under Cleric" stops being a fact. So the run records which loadouts seeded it *and* whether you then changed anything, and the line becomes "Seeded from … then edited". The flag is computed, not set, so it can't drift.

## Where I got it wrong first

You caught four things I'd have shipped: a disclosure instead of a menu, cards too big, no way to add a line from scratch, and truncated fields. All fixed. The last one took three passes because flexbox wraps on the *basis* before it shrinks anything — so the fix was the basis, not the min-width.

**One thing still doesn't fit.** A weapon row is five controls, and its two longest names overflow by a few pixels. Every other row across all fourteen loadouts is clean. Widening them means wrapping the row or clipping the select, and I think both are worse — but say the word and I'll trade differently.

## Two things outside what you asked

American spellings the September sweep missed — six, all in comments. `cancelled()` in the workflow stays, being GitHub's own function name.

And `.entire/` appeared mid-session from a checkpoint tool and got swept into a commit by `git add -A`. I pulled it back out and left it untracked — whether that config belongs in the repo is your call, not a side effect of a spelling fix. It's also adding an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer to commit messages, which you may not want given your no-trailers rule.

content.text:
Both answers are no, and for the same reason.

## Talisman slots via attributes

No. `player.*` exposes exactly eight attributes — `vigor`, `mind`, `endurance`, `strength`, `dexterity`, `intelligence`, `faith`, `arcane`, each 1–99. They're the level stats and nothing else.

The full numeric surface is fifteen names: those eight, plus `player.speed`, `game.speed`, `game.fps`, `player.newGame`, `player.incomingDamage`, `player.outgoingDamage`, and `player.spiritAsh`. No slot count of any kind. Talisman pouches aren't an item, a flag, an attribute, or a press — there's no path to them.

## All maps

Also no, and I checked the way the game names them rather than the way I'd guess: no `fragment` entries beyond `Ruin Fragment` and `Scadutree Fragment`, and zero hits for `limgrave`, `liurnia`, `caelid`. The four items matching "map" — `Cross Map`, `Meeting Place Map`, `New Cross Map`, `Weathered Map` — are quest items, not region fragments.

**But the thing you actually want may already be there.** The all-graces switch you spotted is `travel.showAllGraces`, and it's a *flag*, not a grace list — every site of grace becomes visible and warpable. Combined with `warp.grace` (travel to any grace by name, from a 419-entry list), that delivers the practical benefit of a full map: you can go anywhere without having walked there. What stays unrevealed is the drawn map itself — terrain, roads, icons.

So a "Give the Lands Between" loadout is possible today as:

```yaml
- { op: flag.set, args: { name: travel.showAllGraces, value: true } }
```

That's one line and it isn't a gift, so it doesn't need `once`. Want me to add it? It's a different kind of setup from the seven — it changes what the world does rather than what you're holding — so it might read better named for travel than for leveling.

One caveat on all of this: I'm reading this repo's snapshot of the tool's surface, which says it was written **against the control tab, September 2026**. If TarnishedTool has added operations since, the snapshot wouldn't know. `scripts/extract-tool-lists.py` regenerates it from the tool's own resources if you want to confirm against a current build.

=== extract script head ===
"""The names TarnishedTool knows, so the Control panel can offer them.

Run by hand against a checkout of the fork, because the fork is a
separate repository and this is not a thing that changes between
releases of the game:

    python scripts/extract-tool-lists.py ../TarnishedTool-runlog-integration

The panel asks somebody to name a grace, an item or a weapon, and
before this it asked with an empty box: the names are exact, the game
has four hundred of each, and there was nowhere to look them up
without leaving the run. The lists come from the tool's own resources,
which is the same data it will match the name against when the frame
arrives, so a name the panel offers is a name the tool accepts.

MIT, from borgCode/TarnishedTool by Shilkey. The names themselves are
Elden Ring's.
"""
import json, sys, os
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

root = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "../TarnishedTool-runlog-integration"
resx = os.path.join(root, "TarnishedTool", "Properties", "Resources.resx")
out = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "apps", "web", "src", "control", "lists", "tarnishedtool.json")

data = {d.get("name"): (d.findtext("value") or "") for d in ET.parse(resx).getroot().findall("data")}
rows = lambda key: [l.split(",") for l in data[key].splitlines() if l.strip()]

# Graces: dlc flag, area, name, and two numbers the tool resolves itself.
graces = sorted({(r[2].strip(), r[1].strip()) for r in rows("Graces") if len(r) >= 3})

# Everything `item.named` will match against, in the same order the tool
# builds its own pool. Key items only where the tool hands them over
# without an event behind them, which is the ones with no event id.
ITEMS = ["Consumables", "UpgradeMaterials", "CraftingMaterials", "CrystalTears", "Talismans", "Armor", "Arrows", "PotsAndPerfumes", "Sorceries", "Incantations"]
items = {r[2].strip() for key in ITEMS for r in rows(key) if len(r) >= 3}
items |= {r[2].strip() for r in rows("KeyItems") if len(r) >= 7 and r[6].strip() in ("-1", "")}

# Weapons carry how far they reinforce: the ordinary ones to +25, the
# ones on somber stones to +10. The panel holds the level to that.

content.text:
That settles it — and there's a better answer than I gave you.

## What's reachable today

`action.invoke` dispatches by `HotkeyActions` enum name, and `TravelViewModel.RegisterHotkeys()` already registers all of these. **No fork change needed** — our `PRESSES` list just doesn't offer them:

| Name | What it does |
|---|---|
| `UnlockMainGameMaps` | Unlock Base Game Maps |
| `UnlockDlcMaps` | Unlock DLC Maps |
| `UnlockAllMainGameGraces` | Unlock All Main Game Graces |
| `UnlockAllDlcGraces` | Unlock All DLC Graces |
| `UnlockAllMainRemembrancesGraces` / `UnlockAllDlcRemembrancesGraces` | the two AR grace buttons |

The important distinction: **`UnlockMainGameMaps` is a one-shot unlock; `ShowAllMaps` is a toggle.** A setup wants the unlock — a toggle flips whatever the state happened to be, so a run can't know what it got. Same reason the existing `travel.showAllGraces` flag is weaker than `UnlockAllMainGameGraces`: the flag reveals them, the press actually unlocks them.

I verified all 15 of our current press names are real enum members, so the convention holds.

## On talisman slots — still no

That one I'm confident about: `GameOperations.cs` registers exactly fifteen numbers, and the eight `player.*` attributes are the level stats. Nothing in the fork exposes a talisman slot count, and the tool's Player tab has no control for it either.

Let me add the map and grace unlocks and build the setup.

feat(packs): unlock the map and the graces

The Travel tab has six unlock buttons and this app offered none of them,
so I said the tool could not do it. It can, and it always could:
`action.invoke` dispatches by the name of a `HotkeyActions` member, and
`TravelViewModel.RegisterHotkeys` registers every one of these. The
missing piece was this list.

    UnlockMainGameMaps
    UnlockDlcMaps
    UnlockAllMainGameGraces
    UnlockAllDlcGraces
    UnlockAllMainRemembrancesGraces
    UnlockAllDlcRemembrancesGraces

**The unlocks, not the toggles beside them.** `ShowAllMaps` and
`NoMapAcquiredPopup` are registered too and are deliberately left out: a
press that flips a setting leaves a run unable to say what it started
with, where `UnlockMainGameMaps` is the same afterwards however many
times it is pressed.

"Open the Map" is the setup: every map fragment and every grace, so a
run can start where it means to start rather than walking there. The DLC
lines are harmless without the DLC, since the tool refuses a press it
cannot make rather than failing the run.

## A second guard

A press the tool has no action for fails exactly as a misspelled item
does: the string is taken, the tool answers "not registered in this
build", and the run carries on having been handed nothing. Item names
were already held against the tool's lists; presses are now held against
the catalog, which is the nearest thing to that enum living here.

Checked the fifteen presses the catalog already offered against the
fork's enum while writing it. All fifteen are real.

1178 tests, 29 documents validate.
EOF
